NurED commentary: Daṁḍa (revision 3627)

Commentary

A widespread Indo-Aryan word without cognates in Iranian. Earlier hypotheses of Indo-European origin and relation to Gr. δένδρον 'tree' are faced with difficulties on the Greek side (cf. EWA I: 692). The most promising alternative explanation is that the word is of Dravidian origin (cf. DED 3056; see also s.v. *tāṁḍagā), in which case borrowing via Indo-Aryan is the most likely case.

The descendant forms show various divergences from the original distribution of dental and retroflex (dVṇḍ°). Pr. forms like ḍuṇḍ, which have most likely been borrowed via other Nuristani languages, provide a clue that the ḍVnd° forms may have come about via assimilation to ḍVṇḍ°, followed in turn by a dissimilation to ḍVnd°.

The place name Kt. se Ḍuníğil 'Dir Kohistan' may also contain this root.

NurED commentary: *nās(ā̆)- (revision 2074)

Commentary

The Nuristani forms are superficially similar to their Indo-Aryan cognates in the surrounding region, but the Indo-Aryan forms reflect the later Indo-Aryan generalization of various derivatives, such as nastā̆- or nā́sikā-, as their suffixes and stem variation patterns show. The Nuristani forms, on the other hand, could represent the older formation of OIA nā́sā-, YAv. nā̊ŋhā-, a feminine ā stem resulting from reanalysis of the dual form (= OIA nās-ā) of the original PIIr. root noun *(H)nas- ~ *(H)nās- (EWA II: 30), or it could result from an independent thematization of the root noun. The masculine gender in Kt. need not be original (for the other languages the gender of the noun has not been recorded), but if it is, it could point to an independent derivative *(H)nās-a-, which is not attested in the rest of Indo-Iranian. Though there is no fully conclusive proof for this, the word is more likely inherited, also in view of its semantic field (basic body parts).

The Kt. meaning probably results from metaphorical usage of the body part term for landscape/mountain features, a process that has several parallels in Nuristani. For 'nose' in particular, cf. also the similar developments in German (Fels-)nase 'rock outcrop' and Avar meʕer 'nose; mountain'. The original meaning of the Kt. word is preserved in compounds, such as naskór 'face'.

The appurtenance of NKal. naštë́ ~ nāstá is uncertain. The development *st > ẓ št indicates that it is likely an inherited word. In its formation it may be compared with OIA nasta- 'nose' and on the Iranian side with Par. nēšt 'nose' < *nās-ti- (IIFL I: 277). Semantically, cf. Kho. nas 'edge' < nāsā- and nast 'ahead, in front, preceding' < nasta- (BKhoL). Alternatively, a connection with PIIr. *nas- 'to arrive (home)' could also be considered.

Related words borrowed from IA are discussed s.v. MIA *nāsāvuḍa, *nāṣa and *natthā.

NurED commentary: *ċuċama- (revision 3621)

Commentary

The Kt. ne/se a in the first syllable is unexplained, but perhaps comparable to that in tapék/tapkë́ 'rifle' ⇐ Psht. tupák.

The inclusion of the Pr. words in this cognate set is not certain, but they match formally and the identification of the deity Züzúm with Kt. noŋ makes it possible semantically. The correspondence Kt. ċ NKal. ċ ~ Pr. z points to an inherited word with PNur. *ċ.

Even if the Pr. words are not included, Morgenstierne's (1929: 197–198) supposition that these words are early borrowings into Nuristani from an equivalent of OIA śiṁśumā́ra- is difficult to accept, since it would require borrowing from Pre-Proto-Indo-Aryan into Pre-Proto-Nuristani at a time when both still had *ć < PIIr. *ć. The non-matching vocalism and the lack of a correspondence for the ending °āra- of the OIA form introduce additional difficulties.

A connection with the IA forms is possible only under the assumption of a very ancient loanword from an unknown language, independently borrowed into Indo-Aryan (perhaps more than once) and Nuristani. The alternating vowels and suffixes (?) could then be attributed to unknown features of the unknown source language.

NurED commentary: *ċū(kā̆)bār(a)- (revision 2828)

Commentary

An inherited word with PIIr. *ć > ċ preserved only in Dam., whereas all other languages have an IA loanword (MIA *śpāvi) as the usual word for 'porcupine'.

The formation appears to be a compound of an Indo-Iranian word for 'spike, bristle, needle' with a form of *bʰar- 'to carry'. The long vowel in the second element can be taken to point to a nominal *bʰāra- 'load, burden' (as opposed to *-bʰara- 'carrying') having been combined in a bahuvrīhi compound ('having spikes as a load' = 'carrying spikes'). In Middle Iranian (and probably Nuristani, cf. *-bāra-), reflexes of *bʰāra- also appear as adjectival suffixes meaning 'having < *'carrying'. This usage could itself be based on earlier use in bahuvrīhi- compounds, though Schmitt (2014: 138) assumes that an adjectival/agent noun form *bʰāra- in the sense of 'carrying, carrier' existed already in PIIr. and uses this to explain the OP compound asa-bāra- 'rider' as having an original sense of 'having a horse as carrier'.

Pace Morgenstierne (1942: 163) and Turner (CDIAL: T. 12766), the Dam. word is most likely not an inherited cognate of OIA śvāvídh-, since the derivation suggested above provides a better explanation of the phonological form.

NurED commentary: *śpāvi (revision 2744)

Commentary

A certain loanword with an IA palatal development (*ć > ś) and a Northwestern MIA phonological innovation (śv > śp).

Pace Morgenstierne (1942: 163) and Turner (CDIAL: T. 12766), Dam. ċuwā́r 'porcupine' is most likely unrelated to these words.

NurED commentary: *štarwa(ka)- (revision 3553)

Commentary

These words are most likely inherited due to *st > *št. The development of PIIr. *ru̯ > *rw, suggested here by the preservation of *r in most of the daughter forms, is unlike the development *ru̯ > *ww observed by Halfmann (2025: 93–94) in monosyllables. A possible way to reconcile the two is by assuming a role of stress[2] in the development of the cluster: V́ru̯V > V́wwV, but Vru̯V́ > VrwV́.

The Kt. dialect forms result from varying reductions of the cluster *štrw after pre-stress syncope. The se form has a prothetic vowel emerging from labialization/*w.[3]

The suffix formation with *-u̯a-ka- < PIIr. *-u̯an- + *-ka- is most closely matched by the Iranian forms with *-u̯an- and lacks a counterpart in OIA. The presence of the suffix is not immediately obvious in the modern Nuristani forms, but without it the preservation of *-r- and the vowel developments would be difficult to explain.

Commentary notes

  1. ↑ Meaning the secondary Nuristani penultimate stress.
  2. ↑ Cf. Kt. ne ssi-, se vušší- < *sčʷčča- < *sčut-i̯a- in Halfmann (2025: 72). There the se form is most likely incorrectly explained as "probably prefixed".

NurED commentary: *aj̈ā(ra)- (revision 2453)

Commentary

An inherited word with cognates only outside of Indo-Iranian. While Morgenstierne (1954: 162) classified it as "of unknown origin", Hamp (1968: 130) proposed a connection to "Slavic (j)ezero". The form ⟨árzá⟩ printed in Lumsden (1860), which he cites in support of this, is based on a misreading from the original manuscript, which says ⟨āzā⟩ (Lumsden (1859)), and is therefore irrelevant for the etymological interpretation. Nevertheless, Hamp's proposal can be maintained, since *-r- is regularly lost in the relevant position.

The long vowel in the second syllable is best explained if we assume an independent analogical thematization of the original r-stem in pre-Proto-Nuristani, during which the strong stem of the accusative was generalized, in a parallel to the well-known development of this kind in MIA (e.g. OIA ádhvan- way > Pa. addhāna-, cf. von Hinüber 2001: 219). Thus, roughly, *aj̈ar- (nom. *aj̈ā, acc. *aj̈āram) > *aj̈āra- (nom. *aj̈āras, acc. *aj̈āram).

The Kt. w kt form azyú is unexpected and does not agree with the other forms.[2]

Commentary notes

  1. ↑ Could it be a typographical error? It appears in the wordlist directly below the identical tree name azyú.

NurED commentary: *aṁnajja (revision 3543)

Commentary

The shortening of the second vowel is a result of the MIA law of two moras. In the NIA cognates this is reversed by vowel lengthening before geminates, but the syncope in Kt. would only apply to a short *a, which shows that this re-lengthening did not take place in Nuristani.

NurED commentary: *wiċ(aya)n(a)- (revision 3615)

Commentary

An inherited word due to PIIr. *ć > PNur. *ċ.

Turner derives these words from a reconstructed pseudo-OIA form *ut-śiras- (i.e., PIIr. *ud + *ćr̥Has-), citing the parallel of IA forms like OIA ucchīrṣaka- n. n. 'that which raises the head, pillow', Pkt. ussīsa- n. n. 'pillow', but the Nuristani words require a nasal rather than a rhotic in the ancestral form and do not have much in common with the reflexes of PIIr. *ćr̥Has-.

The fact that the Kt. forms have a segmental nasal instead of vowel nasalization is explainable as an analogical generalization of the original non-direct stem ending in *-n̆- (cf. Halfmann 2024a: 134–136).

The Kt. ne form aċén̆ may derive from a different formation *ā-ċayana- with PIIr. *ā instead of *u̯i (cf. OIA ā-śay- 'to lie or rest on', MP āsāy- 'to rest'), though in view of the agreement of all other dialects and languages it is worth considering whether it could instead be explained as an analogical creation (extracted from a prefixed locative?).

NurED commentary: *kārr(ã)- (revision 3314)

Commentary

This word probably went through the stages *karna- > *kārna- > *kārnã- > *kārrã- before the disintegration of the Proto-Nuristani ancestor language. As Hamp (1968: 131–132) has shown, the postulation of an unattested variant *kāra- (as in CDIAL: T. 3056) is not required (and indeed inadmissible) for Nuristani.

Meanings like Kt./NKal. 'tuning peg (of string instrument)', NKal. 'corner, side, bank, edge', A. 'slope' are probably results of metaphorical extension from 'ear' (cf. Prs. gōša 'corner' ← gōš 'ear'), rather than reflections of originally separate etyma.

Gray (1927: 438–440) and Burrow (1973: 132) have proposed that YAv. karəna- 'ear (of daevic beings)' is a loanword from Indo-Aryan, which would make its reconstruction for Proto-Indo-Iranian more doubtful and, as a consequence, lead to the interpretation that Nuristani aligns lexically with Indo-Aryan in this case. However, there are no phonological reasons to identify it as a loanword and a derivate of PIIr. *kárna- survives into modern Iranian languages in the form of NP karr 'deaf' etc. (< *karná- > YAv. karəna- 'deaf', OIA karṇá- 'long-eared') (cf. Tucker 2022: 260). Rather than necessarily implying provenance from a language of foreign enemies, the pejorative connotations of YAv. karəna- (which seem to be absent in the tree name gao-karəna- 'cow's ear') are more likely a result of normal semantic drift, exacerbated by poetic choice and eventual conventionalization (cf. Tucker 2022). The fact that *kárna- 'ear' leaves no descendants in later Iranian, may be due to the Common Iranian replacement by *gʰau̯ša-, the agent noun to *gʰau̯š- 'to hear'.

NurED commentary: *kaṁṭha (revision 3262)

Commentary

An Indo-Aryan word with no etymology beyond OIA (cf. EWA I: 292). The unconditioned retroflexes make it unlikely that this is an inherited Nuristani word. Borrowed from a source without post-nasal voicing, unlike related *kaṁḍhaga 'voice, call, invitation; boundary, edge'. The sense 'invitation' may have previously also existed for this form, if the element kuṭ in Kt. se kúṭ-miẓō̃ 'feast given when effigy was erected [pre-Islamic]' can be interpreted in this way (miẓō̃́ = 'food eaten with bread').

Turner (CDIAL: T. 2680) also reports a Kt. word "kaṭī́" 'sound' from Morgenstierne's field notes, but this is not known from other sources.

NurED commentary: Kāṁḍa (revision 3392)

Commentary

Though the ultimate etymology of OIA kā́ṇḍa- is unclear, given its phonology (with unconditioned -ṇḍ-), it is usually considered to be of non-Indo-European or MIA origin (EWA I: 336–337; KEWA: 197) and it has no cognates in Iranian. It is therefore most likely a loanword from IA in Nuristani. An additional point in favor of this interpretation is that the Nuristani forms only attest the meaning 'arrow', which is not present in the earliest attestations of the word and only develops in the course of IA history.

The feminine gender of the Nuristani forms is unexpected, but paralleled in Pash..

NurED commentary: *khura (revision 3672)

Commentary

An Indo-Aryan word without cognates in Iranian or wider Indo-European (EWA I: 454). Loanword status in Nuristani is additionally likely due to preservation of intervocalic -r- throughout and a particular shift in meaning from 'hoof' to 'foot' that is found only in a subset of Indo-Aryan languages of the surrounding region.

The age of this semantic shift is unclear since the word is unattested in Gāndh.. Areally, it extends from the Kunar group via southern Chitral (including western Shinaic varieties spoken there) to parts of Kohistan and includes even Kashm., but it is not found in Kho., core Sh., Tir. or most of Pash. (Fussman 1972: 273–274). This distribution is most compatible with the assumption of a central innovation that did not reach some peripheral areas.

Notably, in Pr. the reflex of this IA loanword still means only 'hoof', indicating that the word may have first been borrowed in its original sense and only subsequently acquired the meaning 'foot' while Nuristani was still under the influence of IA varieties. This later semantic shift would appear not to have been transmitted to Pr..

The original word for 'foot' is likely preserved in Kt. po etc.

NurED commentary: *baj̈u(ka)- (revision 3175)

Commentary

Morgenstierne (1929: 249) has compared these forms to OIA bahíṣ- 'outside' and bahir-vāsas- 'outer garment', which would imply that they are inherited cognates derived from a PIIr. *baj́ʰiš-, e.g. as *baj́ʰi-ka- or *baj́ʰi-ra- (though IA has only OIA bāhīká- 'being outside, external', Pa. bāhira- 'external', both with long ā). Semantically this is possible, but it is not clear whether the vowel correspondences in the second syllable allow such a derivation. The available A. evidence is phonologically unreliable, but shows no palatalization of z to ž, which would be expected before *i. The assumption of an original *u in the second syllable would be less problematic.

It may therefore instead be preferable to compare the Nuristani forms to the words for 'thick, dense, coarse' listed above, either as PNur. *baj̈u-ka- or as *baj̈u-ra- (~ OIA bahulá-). Semantically, this would be equally possible, since the garment in question is a thick overcoat.[1]

With either derivation, the development PIIr. *j́ʰ > *j̈ would identify these forms as inherited.

Commentary notes

  1. ↑ A potential comparison with OIA bāhú-, YAv. bāzu- 'arm' (cf. PNur. *bāj̈[u]-), which is perhaps semantically connectable via the notion of 'sleeve', runs into issues with the short vowel in the first syllable. The similarity of Mal. baju 'shirt, jacket' would appear to be accidental, even though this word is usually explained as a loanword from Prs. bāzū 'arm' (Blust et al. 2023), so that a parallel borrowing into Nuristani is theoretically not impossible. However, the derivation of the Mal. from Prs. is quite uncertain, since Prs. bāzū is not attested with the meaning 'shirt'. Additionally, if we were to assume that the Nuristani terms are borrowed from Prs., the short vowel in the first syllable would still be unexpected.

NurED commentary: *āċa(ka)- (revision 3081)

Commentary

An inherited word with the characteristic Nuristani development PIE *ḱ > *ċ.

The connection to OIA ˚āśa- was first suggested by Strand (1999b). Morgenstierne (1945a: 229) had earlier proposed a comparison between Kt. pr̆oċ in the sense 'wheel of cheese' and OIA prāśa- (pra-āśa-) 'eating, food' formed from the same root, but this is less convincing (see s.v. for more).

Reconstructability of the root for PIE is doubted by Lubotsky (2010: s.v. aśⁱ) and Cheung (2007: 168). Verbal descendants are not clearly attested in Iranian and also do not survive in Nuristani. Another nominal derivative may be Kt. vanë́ċ 'dish cooked in ghee'.

NurED commentary: *pārċ(wa)- (revision 3710)

Commentary

An inherited word with the characteristic Nuristani development PIIr. *ć > ċ. The Kt. form can formally derive equally well from earlier *pā̆rć° or *prāć°.

The root is most likely PIE *perḱ- 'spotted', which is also contained in the forms and reconstructions cited above (all based on Widmer 2012 and Ginevra 2021), though there is no formation within Indo-Iranian that exactly matches the Nuristani forms. Since the basic meaning is 'spot' and not 'spotted', a possible explanation would be as the reflex of a concrete noun *pórḱu̯o- 'spot' derived from the adjective *porḱu̯-ó- 'having a spot, mark, color' reflected in PGer. *far̵gwa- 'colored'. Here at least a related formation (*pérḱ-u-) is indirectly attested within Indo-Iranian.

The meanings 'flatbread', 'wheel of cheese' could be taken as further semantic developments from 'spot, patch, flat round thing', though Morgenstierne (1945a: 229), citing only the sense '(small) cheese', has compared Kt. pr̆oċ to OIA prāśa- (pra-āśa-) 'eating, food', in which case it would be related to Kt. aċë́ 'dish from flour and ghee'. This appears less likely in view of the more complete lexical data available today, since the semantic spectrum of pr̆oċ seems to be centered around a particular shape rather than the role as food.[3] The different genders of the two groups of senses could – but do not have to – point to separate origins.[4]

Yidgh. plāċ "Kafir cheese" (i.e. 'rennet cheese') is a likely loanword from Kt. (Morgenstierne 1945a: 229). The similarity of Kho. bɫats 'round' (of unclear etymology) is most likely accidental.

Commentary notes

  1. ↑ A semantic development *'food' > *'bread' > 'loaf, wheel of cheese' > 'flat round object' could theoretically be assumed in order to uphold Morgenstierne's etymology (cf. Germ. Käse-laib 'wheel of cheese' with Laib < PGer. *hlaibaz 'bread'), but it would be less straightforward than the explanation suggested here.
  2. ↑ The only source for masculine gender in the sense 'spot' is Strand's (1999b) wordlist, where the entry with the translation "rounded symmetrical design" and the compounds referring to shoe soles are not marked as feminine, which implies masculine gender in Strand's system of notation.

NurED commentary: *aċru(kā̆)- (revision 3263)

Commentary

The Kt., A. and Pr. forms are identified as inherited words by the development PIIr. *ćr > PNur. *ċr > Kt. c̣, Pr. č, A. str.

Pace Turner (CDIAL: 919), A. str does not result from metathesis tsr > str. The -t- is more likely an intrusive occlusion between s (< *ċ) and r. IA cognates could independently develop the same kind of occlusion (a typologically common sound change), so that Turner's (CDIAL: 919) sociolinguistically implausible assumption that such forms in IA are borrowed from A. is not required.

NKal. üṣǘk tear, on the other hand, is more likely an IA loanword due to the development PIIr. *ćr > śr > ṣ (see s.v. MIA *aṣṣu).

Nuristani agrees with Indo-Iranian in general in showing a reflex of PIE *h₂eḱru-. Agn. (Toch. A) ākär and Lith. ãšara could also be derived from such a PIE reconstruction, but other IE branches have apparent cognates with different onsets (e.g. Hitt. išḫaḫru, Gr. δάκρυ).

NurED commentary: *ankra(ka)- (revision 3440)

Commentary

These words are derived from OIA aṅkura- by Turner (CDIAL: T. 109), following a proposal by Morgenstierne (1934: 80), but while this is formally possible for the Kt. forms (if < *ankura-ka-), the A. form necessarily points to an original cluster *kr, as is hinted at by Morgenstierne's (1934: 80) reconstruction "*aŋk(u)ra-". The vowels of the Pr. form also do not match *ankura-, as this would be expected to produce **ükǘ.

The meaning *'hooked' is in any case not demonstrable for OIA aṅkura-, which is only attested in the meaning 'sprout' (EWA III: 5), despite formally similar Gr. ἀγκύλος 'bent', OHG angul '(fish)hook' (EWAhd.: s.v. angul). A connection of the Nuristani forms to the PIE root *h₂enk- 'to bend' (LIV₂: 268) nevertheless does appear likely. The vocalism of the Pr. form probably necessitates the reconstruction of a nasal in the root.

A derivate with the suffix/sequence *-lo- (> PIIr. *-ra-) attached directly to the root is attested in Gr. [Hesych.] ἀνκλόν 'curved, bent' ('σκολίον') and perhaps indirectly reflected by Agn. (Toch. A) añcäl 'bow' (Kremmer 2021: 10-11). Otherwise a -ro- adjective *h₂n̥k-ro- with restored root nasal (cf. AiGr II, 2: 853) would also be imaginable. Since both of these derivates have no direct equivalents within Indo-Iranian, the word is likely inherited. Another derivate from the same root is NKal. ẓ ãkë́ 'hook'.

See also MIA *ākaṛī.

NurED commentary: *angusta- (revision 3541)

Commentary

Despite striking parallels in the surrounding NIA languages, this set seems to be inherited since there is no reflex of retroflex -ṣṭ- (Kt. has ṣt < *-ʷšt-, not ṣṭ < *-ṣṭ-). Though there is clear evidence for de-retroflexion/palatalization of c̣ (< kṣ) by following -i-/-y- in the northwestern NIA languages (cf. Halfmann 2025: ), such evidence is lacking for ṣṭ (Pash. has ṣṭhy > ṣ ~ č, but not > **st or **št), so that the Nuristani forms cannot be derived from hypothetical MIA forms like *aṁguṣṭhya(ga) or *aṁguṣṭhiya, which probably underlie the NIA cognates.

Nevertheless, it is possible that the IA formation exerted a semantic influence on the Nuristani forms, which are perhaps calqued on the IA model. This would be especially likely if the presumable PNur. stem *angusta- originally also meant 'thumb' rather than 'finger', like in IA. Unfortunately we have no further evidence either way. The IA meaning 'thumb' is still reflected in Kashm. nyọ̆ṭhᵘ ~ nyoṭhᵘ 'thumb-ring', but the development of 'thumb-related' > 'finger ring' already shows up in Pkt. aṅgutthala 'finger ring' < *aṅguṣṭhya-la-. This semantic change may itself have been supported by Iranian influence, since *angušta- generally means 'finger', not 'thumb', in Iranian and terms for 'ring' are generally derived from this word in Iranian languages.

Cf. also Kt. w aŋúštri and Pr. wogíg.

NurED commentary: *(d)mān(a)- (revision 3725)

Commentary

Turner (CDIAL T.560) derived the Nuristani words for 'house' from the Vedic form amā́ 'at home' (loc.sg.), but this is phonologically impossible (the final syllable would be lost and the l in Pr. remains unexplained). Morgenstierne's (1929: 241) derivation < "*ā-māta- 'built'" is also phonologically problematic, as the correspondence Kt. ne u ~ w/se o in the second syllable appears to require an original following nasal and the l in Pr. again remains unexplained. It is also semantically less straightforward than the derivation from PIIr. *dmāna- 'house' proposed here

There are no necessary phonological reasons why this set of words would have to be considered inherited, but the cognates are universally found throughout the family and the attestations outside of it, in neighboring Shum. and GB (both āma 'house'), are isolated among their relatives. Other NIA languages have reflexes of OIA gr̥há- in the meaning 'house' (cf. also NKal. gar 'house' ⇐ IA), whereas mā́na- 'house' is not attested in post-Vedic literary IA and only has reflexes meaning 'nest'/'spiderweb' in some northwestern NIA languages (cf. CDIAL T. 10042 and the IA-derived doublet NKal. mr̩̆ 'nest'). The Shum. and GB words could be parallel IA formations of ā + mā́na-, but most likely they are borrowings from Nuristani, since already the closest relatives Gṛan. and Ning. have ge < gr̥há- instead and the Nuristani development of PIIr. *ā to a preposition and further into a local prefix (cf. Degener 1998: 139, Halfmann 2024a: 227) seems to be unparalleled in IA (cf. Reinöhl 2016).[4] Since the forms are synchronically not treated as containing a local prefix, it is necessary to assume that the local prefix was reanalyzed as a fixed part of the word, as in German das Zuhause 'the home' < zu Hause 'at the house'.

The reconstruction of *d at the beginning of the proto-form hinges on the question of whether the l in Pr. ëmë́l reflects a metathesized *d (i.e., *ā-nmāda- < *ā-dmāna-) or whether it results from nasal dissimilation in the sequence *mVn.

Pace Strand (1999b), Kt. se samó 'dance' etc. does not belong here.

Commentary notes

NurED commentary: *ruċy(a)- (revision 3287)

Commentary

Following Morgenstierne (1949: 279), these Nuristani forms have generally been held to be cognates of OIA vrīhi- 'rice', deriving from a presumable PIIr. form **u̯rīj́hi-. This etymology is accepted, e.g., by Turner (CDIAL: T. 12233) and Kümmel (2017: 281, 283). However, it fails both formally, as PIIr. *u̯r- produces Kt. br̆- (cf. br̆e 'flour' < *wre[w]i[ta]-, br̆iċë́- ~ br̆ëċé- 'to spin' < *wriċ-),[1] and semantically, as rice and barley have little in common either in terms of physical attributes or of cultivation techniques. Speakers of ancestral Nuristani varieties are also unlikely to have had knowledge of rice agriculture and its terminology, which was probably borrowed into already diversified Indo-Iranian languages after its arrival in South Asia.

On the other hand, the Khotanese, Tumshuqese and Khwarezmian terms mentioned above produce a plausible formal and semantic match. Kümmel (2017: 281; against Bailey 1979: 367, NEVP: 10) is probably justified in separating these Middle Iranian words from various New Iranian terms that seem to derive from something like *arpućya- or *arpaćya- (e.g. Psht. orbə́ša (f.), Sangl. vərvə́s 'barley', Mnj. āršíya 'type of barley (from central Nuristan)' [NEVP: 10, G-Mnj]).

The correspondence Kt. ċ ~ Pr. z can theoretically derive from a PNur. *j̈ in secondary word-final position, as required for the 'rice' etymology, but its source may just as well be a PNur. *ċ < PIIr. *ć (whence also Khot. and Khwar. s). Some difficulties remain with regard to the vowel development. The i Kt. could derive from an earlier *i, but it may also show the same kind of umlaut before a palatal consonant as in Kt. ◊ piš 'flower' < MIA puśśa. This umlaut would then have to have happened early enough to prevent the outcome ẓ < *r- |_*u. The Pr. form shows additional suffixing and syncope followed by cluster reduction (*rċ/rz > z) and vowel prothesis. Since the prothetic vowel is not a central vowel and has a different quality than the second syllable, it is likely that it reflects the quality of the original root vowel, which would indicate an original *u as the more likely reconstruction.

This matches the Khot. form and also provides a plausible ultimate etymology from the Indo-Iranian root *rau̯ć- ~ *ruć- 'to shine' (OIA rúś-ant- 'shining, bright', Khot. rrus- 'to shine', harśśäñi 'bright' < *fra-ruć-ya-).[2] However, the formation in Nuristani must be different from Khot. – while Khot. s is incompatible with an original cluster *ći̯, the Nuristani forms are best explained from a derivate *rući̯a-, which would account for the umlaut and masculine gender in Kt. and the i in Pr.. The Khwar. and Tumsh. vocalism is then more difficult to reconcile. The form ⟨rsy⟩ (pl.) originally compared to the Khot. form by Henning (1956: 435), was corrected to ⟨rysy⟩ in Henning (1958: 114, fn. 9 - "rysy wahrscheinlich statt rsy 'Gerste' zu lesen"). While a spelling with no written vowel would have been compatible with the assumption of a root vowel u, the spelling with ⟨y⟩, which also appears in the singular, would rather point to ī or e. Umlaut of *ū̆ > ī̆ seems, however, to be otherwise unattested in Khwar.. The vocalism of the Tumsh. form is already unexpected when compared to closely related Khot.. This issue is also discussed by Ogihara & Ching (2024) and Halfmann (2026: 298).

The word for 'barley' in southern Nuristani languages is probably borrowed from IA, see s.v. MIA yava.

  1. ↑ The variant **wr̆iċ cited by Morgenstierne (1949: 279) is not confirmed anywhere and seems to be a notation error. If it existed, it would still be phonologically incompatible with PIIr. *u̯r-.
  2. ↑ Barley fields are notable for their comparatively light color and the shining effect produced by the long awns reflecting the sunlight.

NurED commentary: *mālaga (revision 1788)

Commentary

Given its Dravidian origin, this is a certain loanword, which can also be deduced from the presence of l in all languages.

NurED commentary: *mālā (revision 3661)

Commentary

The presence of l in all languages shows that this is a loanword.

NurED commentary: *mā(r)čč(a)- (revision 2261)

Commentary

It is not easy to decide whether this set of words is inherited from PIIr. or borrowed from IA, since similar forms are attested in Gāndh. and neighboring NIA. However, the vowel length in Nuristani tips the balance in favor of inheritance. Vowel length also appears in the Shum. cognate māċ, but there it appears next to length in words like mā̃z 'middle' < MIA majjha < OIA mádhya- and therefore most likely results from a NIA compensatory lengthening during the loss of geminates. In Nuristani no such general lengthening can be observed (cf. Kt. pi-míč 'in the middle', not **pë-móč). The Nuristani length can therefore plausibly be attributed to Proto-Nuristani lengthening in the context *V́rC (see the Historical Phonology). This process could not have applied to a borrowed MIA form macca, which no longer contained an r. Based on this reasoning, Dam. mač 'husband', with its short a, cannot be a Nuristani word, but is of Indo-Aryan origin.

NurED commentary: *muṁdha (revision 2877)

Commentary

A certain loanword, given the reflex of the IA development r̥H > ūr (cf. the inherited doublet *mārrānik(a)-).

It is not likely that Tr. modá 'neck' belongs here (as proposed by CDIAL: T. 10247), as this would entail an etymological separation from very similar words for 'neck' in the neighboring languages, on which see s.v. MIA *maṁdaga.

NurED commentary: *mārrānik(a)- (revision 2812)

Commentary

The phonological form of this word can best be explained proceeding from a thematized form *marrāna- based on the accusative *mr̥Hdʰānam of PIIr. *mr̥Hdʰan- 'head' (cf. Pkt. muddhāṇa- < OIA mūrdhán-). The attested forms would then reflect a vr̥ddhi derivative from this form, which accords well with the presence of the suffix *-ika- and the derived meaning 'neck' < *'belonging to the head' (cf. AiGr II, 2: 309, 311).

The development of *r̥H > *ar identifies this as an inherited word (cf. Halfmann 2025: 90–99). While Iranian languages only have reflexes of this word with the prefix ka-, it appears to have been used without a prefix in the pre-history of Nuristani, as also in IA. The prefixation is thereby identified as a specifically Iranian innovation.

The final ŋ in the Kt. se forms is an intervocalic development (cf. Halfmann 2024a: 79) apparently generalized to the direct case from the forms with case suffixes.

Cf. the borrowed etymological doublet *muṁdha.

NurED commentary: *warri(ya)- (revision 1950)

Commentary

Since Morgenstierne (1929: 284), these Nuristani forms have been connected with PIE *u̯erh1- 'to say' (Gr. εἴρω). Based on this, Turner (CDIAL: T. 11327) reconstructed a Pseudo-OIA form *vari- 'speech', but this could not account for the -r-, which, in an inherited word, should be dropped in intervocalic position. His proposal of connections with OIA varṇa- 'sound, syllable' and vā́ṇī- 'voice, sound' is doubtful, as the former is more likely a specialized use of varṇa- 'type, color' and the latter already appears as vāṇī- in the R̥gveda, which makes it rather implausible to assume a reduction from *varṇī vel sim., as would be required for a connection with the other words (cf. KEWA III: 154, 184). It is also difficult to reconcile with the laryngeal which is nowadays reconstructed in PIE *u̯erh1-.

On the other hand, a connection with the Indo-European word for 'word', which likely contains the same PIE root, could account for the -r- as a reflex of *-rr- < *-rd-. The only issue with this explanation is that this etymon does not otherwise appear in Indo-Iranian. Though the Kt. forms could equally well descend from a form with PIIr. *ar or *r̥ in the first syllable, in A. the development to *-rr- would not be expected if the root had *r̥ (cf. A. židí < PIIr. *j́hr̥dai̯a-). A reconstruction with *ar is therefore more likely. The final vowel may reflect a suffix *-iya- or *-ika-.

The suffixes Wakh. -wor, Kho. -war, which appear in language names, have sometimes been connected with the Nuristani forms, but they are most likely unrelated and ultimately borrowed from NP -wār(ī) '-like' (as in, e.g., šēr-wār 'lion-like' [Šāhnāma]) (Steblin-Kamenskij 1999: 391). This suffix is attested since the Middle Iranian period (e.g. MP šāh-wār 'like a king') (see Durkin-Meisterernst 2014: 182) and has been adopted for language names in various cases, e.g. in dialectal Tajik vanǰi-vorí 'in Vanji' = "like the Vanjis" (Steblin-Kamenskij 1999: 391) and (as a loanword) in Domari ḍōm-wāri 'the Domari language', tat-wāri 'the Arabic language' (Matras 2012: 4). Horn (1893: 240) separates it etymologically from homonymous -wār 'bearing' < *-bāra- (as, e.g., in NP umēd-wār 'hopeful'), but Durkin-Meisterernst (2014: 182) makes no such distinction. The Nuristani forms, by contrast, are not suffixes, but frequently appear in independent use. They also cannot derive from a form with long *ā in the first syllable.

NurED commentary: *nāṁga (revision 2702)

Commentary

This group of words originates in a MIA form with early "nasal condensation" (cf. Halfmann 2023b: 330), which has resulted in the preservation of the intervocalic -g-. If the condensing nasalization was moraic, this word can be taken as evidence that "nasal condensation" applied after the Two-Mora Rule.

There are no necessary phonological reasons that would identify these words as borrowed, but the cognates of OIA nāgá- outside of IA mean 'naked' and not 'snake' and other words for snake are more common in the earliest OIA texts, so that the existence of a Nuristani cognate in the meaning 'snake' is not very likely. Additionally, the Nuristani terms appear only in the specialized mythological sense and not as ordinary words for 'snake', which makes it even more likely that they are loanwords.

It is not surprising that the IA word was borrowed only in religious and mythological senses, since in Hinduism "the word for the divine snake is nāga and "worship of the nāga deities associated with water" is one of the well-established forms of Hindu snake worship (Jacobsen 2009: 711). As Jacobsen (2009: 712) explains, "nāgas are connected to water [...] They inhabit lakes and rivers" and "are associated with weather phenomena such as rainstorms and lightening [sic]". These are the same spheres occupied by the etymologically corresponding mythological beings of Nuristani pre-Islamic religion.

The Pr. deity Züzúm, who is identified with Kt. Noŋ, derives his name from an inherited word for *'large reptile', but this may originally have been a calque on the IA word, especially since he is also a god of tempests fitting into the mythological sphere of the nāgas of Hinduism.

The appearance of nāgas in Nuristani pre-Islamic mythology is compatible with the thesis of Halfmann (2023b) that this mythology is largely derived from post-Vedic Hindu models, since nāgá- as the word for 'snake' appears only from the Brāhmaṇas onwards, whereas the earlier Vedic words for snake are áhi- and sarpá- (Jacobsen 2009: 711).

NurED commentary: *nāṁdha (revision 3412)

Commentary

The "cranberry morpheme" Kt. nan-, Pr. nën- can be derived from a MIA descendant of OIA nāthá- with post-nasal voicing (cf. Salomon 1999: 129–130; Schoubben 2024: 395–398) applying after "nasal condensation" (cf. Halfmann 2023b: 330), though interference between the originally unrelated roots nāth- 'to seek refuge' and nādh- 'to be in distress' is also attested starting in OIA times (EWA II: 34).

Assuming that this etymological derivation is correct, the post-nasal voicing would not be expected in case of an inherited word.

NurED commentary: *maṁdaga (revision 3401)

Commentary

These forms are likely borrowed from IA since they show evidence of the late MIA development NN > ND, which is not universal in Nuristani or even throughout the IA loan vocabulary. The geographic distribution of the cognate forms in only the southern Nuristani varieties along with neighboring NIA makes it additionally likely that they are loanwords.

Contra Halfmann (2023b: 349), there is no connection to Kt. min 'forehead' etc.

Contra Turner (CDIAL: 9732), Kt. marẽ́yk 'neck' etc. also have to be separated from this group.

NurED commentary: *aṣṣu (revision 2987)

Commentary

Due to the sound development PIIr. *ćr > ṣ the NKal. form does not fit with the inherited Nuristani reflexes of PIIr. *Háćru- discussed s.v. PNur. *aċru[kā̆]-. The development śr > ṣṣ is well-attested in Gāndh., but the nearest IA neighbors in fact have different developments (OIA śr > Pash. ir, GB nɬ). Borrowing from the more easterly literary dialect in MIA times seems possible, though this particular word is not attested in a conclusive spelling. The final -k in NKal. points to additional (diminutive) suffixation.

NurED commentary: *acchi (revision 3221)

Commentary

Many regional NIA languages have forms resembling those of the Nuristani languages, but the Nuristani forms differ from those in most surrounding IA languages in reflecting a nasal second syllable. In neighboring IA languages this is only found in GB and Shum.,[1] but these languages appear to reflect an original *ī̆ in the second syllable, whereas the vowel correspondence in the second syllable of the Nuristani forms excludes the reconstruction of an original *ī̆.

Following the argumentation of Halfmann (2025: 66–75), the č in the Nuristani forms cannot be considered a regular inherited outcome of PIE *kʷs that would correspond to OIA *kṣ. The Nuristani forms other than Tr. could in theory reflect an original palatal affricate from a formation like PIE *h₃ekʷ-en- (cf. NIL: 371), but such a formation is otherwise not directly attested within Indo-Iranian.

Several of the surrounding IA languages have palatal affricates (or dental affricates developed out of palatals) reflecting OIA kṣ in this word. These result in some cases from mergers of earlier c̣ and č in č (e.g. in Southeastern Pash.), in other cases from secondary palatalizations of the retroflex affricate arising from OIA kṣ by a following i (cf. Halfmann 2025: 66–69). The stem of the Nuristani forms can therefore be considered a loanword from IA. The contrastive retroflex in the Tr. form, still doubted by Halfmann (2025: 68, fn. 84), has now been confirmed in an interview with a native speaker and strongly indicates borrowing from IA. Variation between a retroflex and a palatal reflex of OIA kṣ occurs even within the closely related Kunar group, where GB and Shum. have ċ < *č, but Ning. and Gṛan. have c̣. This could point to a parallel persistence of two variants, possibly arising from paradigmatic variation (inflectional forms with and without following *i), until rather recent times. It is possible that both variants were at one point borrowed into all Nuristani languages, but it is also possible that the retroflex variant only ever entered Tr..

The suffix of the Nuristani forms remains to be explained. Halfmann (2025: 68, fn. 84) proposes that an inherited ending *-āni equivalent to Vedic OIA nom./acc. pl. -ā́ṇi could have been added to the borrowed stem, but the exact process of how this could have happened is difficult to motivate. An alternative explanation would be that the Vedic plural ending -ā́ṇi persisted in earlier IA languages of the region and thence entered into Nuristani as part of a paradigm nom.sg. *acchi, nom./acc. pl. *ac̣c̣hāṇi ~ *acchāni. However, in other regions this ending seems to have already been lost by the MIA period.

Commentary notes

  1. ↑ S. "ac̣hē̃" is not confirmed by Buddruss (1967: 80) who noted ẽc̣hī́, which agrees with the audio recording of Liljegren et al. (2021)

NurED commentary: *kaṭṭigaraga (revision 1786)

Commentary

The reconstruction *kaṭṭi-° presupposed by the attested forms is not directly derivable from OIA kr̥ti-°, from which we would expect something like **kiḍi-°. Instead they more likely reflect a vr̥ddhi form *kārtikara- 'belonging/relating to a sorcerer/magician' derived from kr̥ti-kara-. This adjectival form then seems to have been re-nominalized in the meaning 'sorcerer/magician'. The long vowel of the root syllable is shortened in accordance with the MIA rule of two moras.

The semantic association of the root kar- 'to do' with magic strongly indicates that the word is borrowed from Indo-Aryan, where this association is well attested.

NurED commentary: Vāṇiya (revision 3427)

Commentary

The characteristic northwestern MIA development -j- > -y- identifies this group of forms as loanwords.

Functionally, the development is similar to that of -pāla-(ka-) 'guardian' as a final member of compounds, which became a versatile nominal suffix over the course of IA history, referring to people associated with the base of derivation (Négyesi 2005) and was also borrowed into Nuristani (see pālaga). A comparable semantic development (though with much more limited productivity) happened with the English word/suffix (-)monger, which was extended from contexts like fish-monger to formations like war-monger.[1]

Judging from the overlapping semantic spectrum of the comparable suffixes in GB and Pash.,[2] it is possible that the functional reanalysis was already completed in the IA source language when the element entered Nuristani.

The origin of the Kt. feminine form is not fully clear. Perhaps it is identical with the feminine form of vo/vay 'having', secondarily associated with a form that was originally only masculine.

The derivation of Pr. wuni from PIIr. *-u̯ant- 'having' proposed by Buddruss & Degener (2015: 844) is phonologically problematic. It seems more likely that the suffix is borrowed from Kt., as proposed here, with specialization of its function to that of marking ownership and some functional convergence with the proprietives of the other Nuristani languages (Kt. vo/vay, NKal. oda/odi).

See also MIA *vāṇijja from the same root.

Commentary notes

  1. ↑ While such a development is plausible in general, it is not necessarily the case that all functions of all the attested suffixes are etymologically derived from MIA vāniya. Some of them could be due to secondary homonymy with other etyma.
  2. ↑ The functional spectrum of the Pash. suffix is not well-documented enough for definite conclusions about its etymology.

NurED commentary: *vāṇijjā̆ (revision 3465)

Commentary

The phonological development gives no clear hints as to the inheritance status of these forms, but since the word family of OIA vaṇíj- 'merchant' is very common in later IA, but absent from Iranian, it is overall quite likely that they are IA loanwords in Nuristani (thus also CDIAL: T. 11230, 11233).[1]

Morgenstierne's (1973e: 234) hypothesis that Kt. vr̆ẽč results from contamination of OIA vikrīṇāti 'sells' with the etymon of H/U becnā 'to sell', is not necessary. Since the Kt. w form requires long *ā in the first syllable, MIA vāṇijjā̆- < OIA vāṇijyā̆- is the more likely source than the related synonym MIA vaṇijjā- < OIA vaṇijyā́- with a short root vowel.

The denominal verb stems appear to have been secondarily formed after final devoicing.

See also MIA vāṇiya from the same root.

Commentary notes

  1. ↑ It may also be noted that at least in recent centuries the practice of trade has been considered uncharacteristic of Nuristani culture (see Cacopardo & Cacopardo 2001: 213, fn. 367; Azar 2006: 8, fn. 25).

NurED commentary: *maṁdhānigā (revision 3597)

Commentary

An IA loanword with post-nasal voicing (cf. Salomon 1999: 129–130; Schoubben 2024: 395–398). For derivatives of the same root without post-nasal voicing, see Kt. mëté-, mut.

A connection of the A. word and NKal. wg ⟨mũdˈāṛu⟩ 'stirring stick' with Panj. madā̀ṇī and Psht. mandāṇú ~ mandāṛú (m.) 'churn' [⇐ IA] was first proposed by Morgenstierne (1934: 98; 1954: 276).[1] NKal. wg ⟨mũdˈāṛu⟩, which has not been recorded in later sources or in other dialects, is semantically and phonologically closer to the Pashto form, and therefore more likely a recent loan from Pashto, whereas the other forms are more likely older loanwords taken directly from MIA.

As for the semantic development 'churning stick' > 'walking stick', it may be significant that butter churning in Nuristan is done by shaking an inflated goatskin in one's lap, without the use of wooden sticks. This could explain why the word was only borrowed with a sense referring to a secondary use of the object.

Commentary notes

  1. ↑ Morgenstierne (1954: 276) cites "Pnj. madhāṇā". The word madā̀ṇā is recorded in PUPED only in the sense 'a type of grass – Dectiloctenium egypticum' (probably meaning Dactyloctenium aegyptium). However, this grass is presumably named after its resemblance to the end of a churning stick and is etymologically the masculine counterpart to madā̀ṇī.

NurED commentary: *ċċā(r)k(a)- (revision 3524)

Commentary

If not of onomatopoetic or otherwise secondary origin, this word is most likely inherited, due to the correspondence Kt. ċ ~ A. ċ ~ Pr. ċ, which points to a PIE palatal cluster like *tḱ or *ḱs (cf. Halfmann 2025: 69–72).[3] The final k in all three languages indicates an earlier consonant cluster, possibly with a plosive or *r preceding k.[4]

The number of known PIIr. roots that are compatible with these requirements is small. If PIE *pḱ developed along the same lines in Nuristani as *tḱ and *ḱs, which could so far not be proven (cf. Halfmann 2025: 76, 79), then a connection with PIE *pḱer- > PIIr. *pćar (whence Old Iranian *fšar-) may be possible. The adjective would then be a *-ka- formation based directly on the root (*pćar-ka- 'shameful, harmful'), morphologically comparable to *suš-ka- 'dry' ← *sau̯š- 'to dry' (cf. Degener 1989: 181–182). The original quantity of the root vowel in such a reconstruction could be either *a or *ā due to regular Nuristani lengthening of stressed *a before *rC.[5]

Commentary notes

  1. ↑ The Pr. form could theoretically be borrowed from Kt., but this is less likely for the A. form. The A. form with ċ rather than s excludes a reconstruction with single PIIr. *ć.
  2. ↑ The A. form with k rather than Ṽk excludes a reconstruction with PIIr. *nk.
  3. ↑ In general, r-metathasis to the preceding onset is expected, but it is likely that *ċċ, unlike single *ċ, could not form a cluster with a following *r, so that the *r would be dropped instead.

NurED commentary: *kaligā (revision 3731)

Commentary

An Indo-Aryan loanword due to preserved l in Kt.. There are no clear cognates outside of IA (EWA I: 321–322).

NurED commentary: *tāṁḍagā (revision 1823)

Commentary

A widespread Indo-Aryan word of possible Dravidian origin. The apparent switch of dental and retroflex in Kt. is reminiscent of that seen in ḍun 'stick' ⇐ MIA *daṁḍī.

NurED commentary: Piṁḍa (revision 3290)

Commentary

The wide distribution of this word in Indo-Aryan, along with its peculiar ṇḍ, make it likely that it is a loanword. In accordance with the OIA form, the original root vocalism would appear to be i. Some of the forms are compatible with this, but the vocalism of some of the others points rather to a rounded vowel. It has been suggested that a variant *puṇḍa- could be responsible for some later IA forms. This form is unattested in OIA, unless it is the root of puṇḍárīka- 'lotus flower' (*puṇḍa 'lump' referring to the bulbous blossom?) and/or puṇḍ(r)a- 'mark, sign, sectarian mark on the forehead' (*puṇḍa 'lump' referring to an originally round shape or a clod of marking paste?). Turner (CDIAL: T. 8377) also cites Pkt. puṁḍaïa- 'lump-shaped, globular', poṁḍa-, °aya- 'fruit' in support of this variant.

Berger (1955: 61) has suggested that OIA piṇḍa-, MIA piṁḍa ~ peṁḍa belongs to a group of words from popular registers with uncertain (non-Indo-European?) origins that may have originally (i.e. in a presumable donor language) had short ĕ/ŏ which was substituted in OIA with i/u, but in MIA more accurately with the ĕ/ŏ, which only became available as phonemes at that time. On the other hand, he also proposes a neutralization of the contrast between i and short ĕ before a retroflex syllable coda in MIA (Berger 1955: 62). For this particular word, the assumption of original i and ĕ would therefore both be admissible. Either way, the appearance of another variant with e is not unexpected and need not be due to a vr̥ddhi formation (with MIA e < OIA ai). It is doubtful whether the Nuristani languages ever developed a contrast between long and short e in the course of their history. It is therefore possible that MIA ĕ was simply mapped onto their phoneme /e/. The Nuristani forms above are grouped according to their possible original root vowels.

NurED commentary: *kaṁḍhaga (revision 3399)

Commentary

These words are evidently borrowed from an IA variety with post-nasal voicing, which is known to be present in (parts of) the region since MIA times (cf. Salomon 1999: 129–130; Schoubben 2024: 395–398). This excludes predecessors of the modern-day Gawar-Bati group, but could point to a predecessor of Pashai, though the meaning 'invitation' is not documented there. A cognate without post-nasal voicing (*kaṁṭha) has also been borrowed into Nuristani, possibly from a Gawar-Bati group variety. Notably, the Nuristani forms do not show the NIA lengthening before nasal clusters observable in the Srk. and Pash. forms.

Semantically, a development 'voice' > 'call' > 'invitation (to a feast)' > 'feast' appears to be unproblematic (cf., e.g., Kt. c̣ō ku- 'to call, to invite'). The derivation of the second meaning 'boundary, edge' is more uncertain, but according to Turner (CDIAL: T. 2680) it may be explained as a development from 'throat, neck' via the intermediate meaning 'immediate proximity' attested in the Pañcatantra. Within MIA, Pkt. kaṁṭha- 'border, edge' (cited in CDIAL: T. 2680) attests this meaning.

NurED commentary: *muṭṭa (revision 3727)

Commentary

Widespread parallels in New Indo-Aryan make it likely that this is a loanword.

NurED commentary: *nāsāvuḍa (revision 3657)

Commentary

Dameli nāsr̆ui 'small nose' (FLI-D) may also belong with this set of cognates. The derivation of these words from OIA nāsāpuṭa- was first suggested by Morgenstierne (1940: 246). With this etymology, the Nuristani forms would have to be considered loanwords from IA. A few uncertainties remain, as the Nuristani forms point more directly to *nāsoḍ[a] than *nāsāvuḍa or *nāsāuḍa and the only direct NIA cognate, Gaw. näzōr shows an unexpected phonological form (z instead of s).[3] Perhaps the source for the Nuristani forms was a late MIA form that already showed further vowel contraction than attested Gāndh..

Commentary notes

  1. ↑ The explanation could be offered that this word was borrowed from a variety with sibilant lenition (like literary Gāndh., or Torw., which is spoken directly to the south of Gaw.), before it went as far as to eliminate the sibilant entirely, but this is rather uncertain.

NurED commentary: *nāṣa (revision 3288)

Commentary

This set of words is unusual, since it has direct equivalents in neighboring NIA, indicating that it has most likely come into Nuristani from IA, but also points to a formation that is unattested in OIA, having its closest equivalents in Balto-Slavic. Assuming an IA derivation, the long vowel can only be explained proceeding from an OIA form *nās-ra-, turning into *nāṣṣa- and thence via the two mora rule into *nāṣa.

NurED commentary: *aj̈(ga)- (revision 2991)

Commentary

NKal. -nz- points to an original cluster, but the identification of this cluster as *j̈g can only be made through external comparison. The PIIr. cluster *ds merges into an affricate in Iranian and probably Nuristani, but is reduced to d in OIA (cf. Halfmann 2025: 50).

See Lubotsky (2010: s.v. ádga-) and NIL (207–208) for more on PIE, PIIr. and PCelt. reconstructions and for possible further IE connections. Semantically the Celtic forms show most clearly what the original spectrum of meaning of this word family might have been.

There are many similar, but diverging, Prs. forms with meanings like 'wart, knot in wood, twig, cluster of grapes' and perhaps not all of them belong here (FRZF separates āzax 'wart' from azg 'twig'), but a detailed study would be required to sort out attestations and dialectal distribution. All attested forms are non-Persid, with z for PIIr. *j́⁽ʰ⁾; they also all lack the metathesis *zg > γz seen in NP maγz 'brain' < *mazga-. They could all go back to one etymon (as assumed by Filippone 2011: 213), if forms of the type ā̆zax contain an epenthetic vowel and show final devoicing. The type zax is explainable via NP aphaeresis of a-. With these assumptions, Khwar. ⟨ʾzx⟩, Psht. zə́xa are most likely Persian loans (resp. ⇐ the variants azax and zax; secondary addition of the feminine suffix -a in Psht. is well-attested).

Herzenberg's (2014: 42-43) alternative suggestion that Prs. āzax may be connected with Av. zaṇga- 'ankle', MP zang 'ankle, shank', Oss. zæng/zængæ, OIA jáṅghā- 'lower leg, shank' via a meaning of 'something attached', is implausible (thus also Filippone 2011: 213, fn. 119) and ignores the likely connection of these words to PIE *ǵʰengʰ- to stride (Goth. gaggan) (EWA I: 564, LIV₂: 176).

Khwar. -zγyk '-horned' appears only as the second member of compounds referring to types of livestock and does not by itself mean 'horn', as Henning (1956: 433) implies (cf. Khwar. šw 'horn'). It may be a metaphorical use of an adjective *'-twigged' < *-azg-ika- in specialized livestock terminology, and in this way a genuine cognate.
